before.content_html:
This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

What Is a Geographical Enquiry?

A geographical enquiry is a piece of investigative work that follows a clear cycle. Geographers do not just gather data — they begin with a question, plan how to collect evidence, present and analyse it, then judge what the answer means and how reliable it is. The enquiry process has six recognisable stages, and Eduqas examiners expect you to know all of them.

The cycle is the same whether you are studying a Welsh valley river, a high street in Cardiff or pebble sizes on a Pembrokeshire beach. Knowing the cycle lets you read someone else’s study, spot weak points and design a stronger one of your own.

Key Fact

The six stages are: 1) pose questions, 2) collect evidence, 3) process and present, 4) analyse patterns, 5) draw conclusions, 6) evaluate. The fieldwork paper examines all six.

Stage 1 — Posing Questions and Hypotheses

A good enquiry starts with a clear, focused question linked to a geographical concept. ‘What is the high street like?’ is too vague. ‘How does pedestrian flow change with distance from Cardiff city centre?’ is sharper because it specifies a place, a variable and a relationship.

A hypothesis is a testable prediction. For a coastal study you might write: ‘Pebble size will decrease with distance from a headland because longshore drift sorts material as it moves.’ The hypothesis links observation to a process you have already been taught, so the enquiry tests geographical theory rather than just describing what is there.

Stage 2 — Collecting Evidence

Geographers collect two kinds of evidence. Primary data is gathered first-hand: pebble measurements, pedestrian counts, environmental quality scores, questionnaires you hand out yourself. Secondary data is created by someone else and reused: census data, Environment Agency river-flow records, OS maps and satellite images.

Quantitative techniques generate numbers. They include flow measurements (river discharge, traffic counts), scale measurements (pebble size, gradient with a clinometer), spatial pattern surveys (retail land use) and temporal records (rainfall, temperature). Numbers can be averaged, mapped and graphed.

Qualitative techniques capture opinions and impressions. They include questionnaires with open questions, bi-polar surveys (rating a street from 1 to 5 on cleanliness, safety and noise) and annotated photos or sketches of features. Qualitative data adds the human voice to the numbers.

Sampling: You Cannot Measure Everything

No fieldworker has time to measure every pebble or stop every shopper, so geographers sample. Choosing the wrong sampling method can wreck an enquiry — if your sample is not representative, your conclusion is not either.

Key Fact

Eduqas requires you to know four sampling techniques: random, systematic, opportunistic and stratified. Each is best suited to different fieldwork situations.

Random sampling uses chance — for example, picking grid coordinates with a random number generator before going out. It avoids bias but can leave gaps in awkward locations.

Systematic sampling takes readings at regular intervals — every 10 m along a beach transect, every fifth house on a street. It gives even coverage but can miss patterns that repeat at the same interval.

Opportunistic sampling picks whoever or whatever is available — the next willing shopper, the easiest pebble to reach. It is fast but introduces bias.

Stratified sampling first divides the population into groups (age bands, land-use zones) and then samples from each in proportion. It captures variation but needs background data on the strata before fieldwork begins.

Justifying Sample Size and Method

Eduqas does not just want you to name a method — you must justify it. A river enquiry that takes 10 width readings at every site is more reliable than one that takes 3, but takes longer. A questionnaire with 50 respondents is more representative than one with 10. Justifications should weigh time, accuracy and the risk of bias.

You should also justify the location of your sample sites. For a river study, sites at intervals down a single tributary make a fair test of how channel shape changes with distance from source; sites picked from different rivers would mix variables and make conclusions weaker.

Designing Data Collection Sheets

A data collection sheet is the printed table you carry into the field. Good sheets are simple, pre-printed and have a column for each variable, the date, time, weather and grid reference. Recording these ‘control’ details lets you spot whether unusual readings were caused by rain, rush hour or your own tiredness rather than the geography itself.

The best fieldworkers also carry a clipboard with two copies of the sheet, a pencil (ink runs in rain), a phone for photos with location stamps, and named equipment such as a metre rule, clinometer or quadrat. The risk assessment is finalised before leaving school: tides, traffic, weather, lone-working rules.
before.exam_tip_html: The fieldwork paper often asks you to justify a sampling method or critique someone else’s. Always link your method to its purpose: random sampling reduces bias, systematic gives even coverage, stratified captures variation between groups. Examiners reward the word ‘because’ followed by a clear reason. Avoid generic answers like ‘it is more reliable’ — specify how (larger sample, repeated readings, controlled timing).

before.content_html:
This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

From Numbers to Meaning

Once your data sheets come back from the field, the next stages of the enquiry cycle are processing and presenting the evidence and then analysing it. The goal is to turn a column of raw numbers into a clear pattern that the reader can see, then explain what the pattern means and how strong it really is.

Eduqas examiners reward two skills here. First, you must pick the right kind of graph or map for the data you have. Second, you must use the right kind of statistic to summarise it. The wrong choices hide the pattern; the right ones reveal it.

Key Fact

Match the graph to the data type. Continuous data over time = line graph. Categories = bar chart. Bivariate (two variables) = scatter graph. Spatial pattern = choropleth or proportional symbol map. Frequency distribution = histogram.

Choosing the Right Graph

A bar chart compares totals between separate categories — for example, the number of shops in each retail zone of a high street. The bars do not touch because the categories are independent. A line graph joins data points with a line because the variable changes continuously over time, such as a hydrograph showing river discharge during a storm.

A scatter graph shows the relationship between two variables — for example, distance downstream against river width. A clear upward or downward trend suggests a positive or negative correlation. A histogram shows how often values fall into equal class intervals, such as how many pebbles fall into each 10 mm size band. The bars touch because the data is continuous.

A choropleth map shades areas by value — darker shades for higher values such as deprivation index by ward. They are good for showing patterns across regions but hide variation within a single shaded area. A proportional symbol map uses circles or squares scaled to the value, useful for migration totals or city populations. A flow-line map uses arrows whose width matches the size of the flow, useful for traffic counts or river discharge between gauging stations.

For a high-street pedestrian-flow study, you might place proportional circles on a sketch map of the town — one circle per count point, scaled to the number of pedestrians per minute. The size differences between circles make the pattern obvious at a glance.

Statistics: Central Tendency and Spread

Three measures summarise the ‘middle’ of a data set. The mean is the average. The median is the middle value once the data is sorted. The mode is the most frequent value or category. Each suits different situations: the mean is sensitive to extreme values (one boulder pulls a pebble-size mean upwards), so the median is often a fairer measure for skewed natural data.

Key Fact

Eduqas requires you to know mean, median, mode, range, quartiles and inter-quartile range. The inter-quartile range (IQR) measures the spread of the middle 50% of values, ignoring extremes.

Spread tells you how varied the data is. The range is largest minus smallest, but a single odd reading can stretch it. The inter-quartile range (IQR) is the difference between the upper and lower quartile — the middle 50% — so it ignores outliers and gives a fairer picture. A small IQR means readings cluster tightly around the median; a large IQR means they vary widely.

Identifying Patterns and Trends

Analysis means describing what the graph or map shows and asking why. Useful sentence frames are: ‘The data shows a clear positive correlation between X and Y.’ ‘The pattern is strongest at site 4 and weakens towards site 7.’ ‘Most readings cluster between 25 and 40 mm, with one anomaly at 95 mm.’ Always include numerical evidence from your own results — not just ‘there is a trend’.

A anomaly is a value that does not fit the trend. Geographers do not ignore anomalies — they investigate them. A river-width reading much wider than expected might mean a meander or human modification. A pebble much larger than its neighbours might have been dropped from a cliff fall rather than transported by longshore drift.

Strong analysis links the pattern back to the geographical theory you used to write the hypothesis. If pebble size decreases downstream, that fits the Bradshaw model: attrition smooths and breaks pebbles as they are transported, so they get smaller and rounder away from the source. If pedestrian flow drops with distance from the town centre, that fits the bid-rent model: peripheral shops attract fewer visitors than the central honeypot.

Where the data does not fit the theory, say so. The Eduqas spec stresses that ‘geography can be messy’ — conclusions that admit unexpected results, and try to explain why, score higher than ones that pretend the data was perfect.

Drawing Lines and Trends

On scatter graphs, sketch a line of best fit by eye so the points are roughly balanced above and below it. The slope shows the strength of the relationship. A line of best fit also lets you interpolate — reading off a value within the data — or extrapolate beyond the data. Extrapolation is risky because the trend may not continue.

Quick Self-Check

Before you move on to conclusions, ask three questions. Did you choose the right type of graph for the data? Did you use the right summary statistic, and explain why? Did you describe the pattern with figures from your own results, including any anomalies? If yes to all three, your analysis is on track.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following graph types is most suitable for showing the relationship between distance downstream and river width?
A) Pie chart
B) Choropleth map
C) Scatter graph
D) Population pyramid
Describe two reasons why a geographer might choose to calculate the median rather than the mean of a data set.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• The median ignores extreme values, so a single boulder does not distort the average pebble size.
• The median is the middle value when data is sorted, giving a fairer measure for skewed natural data.
• The mean is pulled towards extreme values, whereas the median is not, so the median better represents the typical value.
• The median is easier to calculate by hand for small samples and does not require summing all values.
[2 marks — accept any two distinct points]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a choropleth map is suitable for showing variations in deprivation by ward across a city.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Choropleth maps shade defined areas (wards) by value, so the city's overall pattern is visible at a glance (1).
• Darker shades for higher deprivation make the pattern easy for a non-specialist reader to follow (1).
• Wards are administrative areas with available data, so values can be compared like-for-like across the city (1).
• Mastering: Three connected points showing why the choropleth fits the spatial pattern.
• Secure: Two clear reasons; pattern visibility addressed.
• Developing: One reason; second descriptive only.
• Emerging: Names the map type but does not explain why it is suitable.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the inter-quartile range and the range as ways of describing the spread of fieldwork data.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points expected; explicit comparative language required. Indicative content:
• Both measure how spread out the values are, but the range uses only the largest and smallest values, whereas the inter-quartile range uses only the middle 50% of values.
• The range is quick to calculate, in contrast to the IQR which needs the data sorted into quartiles before calculation.
• Both can be misleading if not interpreted carefully, but the range can be distorted by a single outlier, similarly to how the mean can be skewed by an extreme value.
• A key difference is that the IQR ignores outliers, whereas the range is dominated by them, so the IQR is more reliable for skewed natural data.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and clear examples.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing or one side undeveloped.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a fieldwork example, explain how analysis can link the patterns shown by graphs to wider geographical theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (any one developed example earns full marks):
• In a downstream river enquiry, scatter graphs of distance vs pebble size typically show a negative correlation. This fits the Bradshaw model: attrition wears pebbles smaller as they are transported downstream.
• Pedestrian flow surveys often show counts dropping with distance from the city centre. A line graph plotted across distance bands fits the bid-rent model, where peripheral shops attract fewer visitors than the central honeypot.
• In a hydrograph study, a steep rising limb after heavy rain indicates a flashy basin. Linking this to land use upstream (urbanisation, deforestation) connects the data to drainage-basin theory.
• In a coastal sediment study, decreasing pebble size with distance from a headland fits longshore-drift theory. Anomalies (a large pebble far from the headland) might be explained by recent cliff fall.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named context, specific theory and clear cause-effect link.
• Secure: Named example with clear theory link and a graph type.
• Developing: Named example but vague theory link.
• Emerging: Generic example with no theory link.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'A clear graph is more important than a careful statistical calculation when presenting fieldwork results.' Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• A well-chosen graph reveals the pattern at a glance — a scatter graph with a line of best fit is more accessible than a paragraph of summary numbers.
• Graphs let the reader spot anomalies and clusters quickly, which is harder to do from raw statistics.
• Spatial patterns in particular (choropleths, flow-line maps) cannot be conveyed by statistics alone — only by visual presentation.
• A confused graph (wrong type, missing axis labels) hides the pattern however correct the underlying numbers are.

Arguments against:
• Statistics let you compare strengths objectively — a small inter-quartile range proves the data is tightly clustered in a way the eye cannot judge from a graph.
• A line of best fit is only meaningful if the relationship is statistically real; without correlation analysis, a sketched line can mislead.
• Reporting just a graph without summary statistics (mean, IQR, percentage change) leaves the conclusion vague.
• Examiners reward use of specific figures from the data, which forces calculation, not just visual estimation.

Justified conclusion expected: graphs and statistics work together — graphs reveal patterns, statistics quantify them, and a strong analysis combines both.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement and two reasoned points each side.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

before.content_html:
Closing the Enquiry Loop

The last two stages of the enquiry process are drawing conclusions and evaluating the work. A conclusion answers the original question using evidence from your data. An evaluation is a critical look back at how you collected and analysed the data: what worked, what did not, and what you would change. Eduqas marks both at the highest tariffs, so this is where strong students separate from weak ones.

A separate part of the Eduqas fieldwork paper also asks you to step beyond your fieldwork and apply geographical thinking to a UK decision-making task. Same skills — evidence, evaluation, judgement — new context.

Stage 5 — Drawing Evidenced Conclusions

A conclusion in fieldwork is a short answer to the original question, supported by figures from your own results. It refers back to the hypothesis, says whether the data supports or rejects it, and links the result to a wider geographical idea.

Key Fact

A strong conclusion follows the pattern: state whether the hypothesis is supported → quote one or two specific figures → link the result to a geographical process or theory. Vague conclusions like ‘the data supports the hypothesis’ lose marks.

For example, a Welsh river study might conclude: ‘Pebble long-axis decreased from a mean of 64 mm at site 1 to 21 mm at site 5, supporting the hypothesis. The pattern is consistent with attrition during transport, where pebbles wear smaller as they are carried downstream.’ The figures and the theory link are what lift this above a description.

Sometimes the data does not support the hypothesis, and that is fine. The Eduqas spec stresses that ‘geography can be messy’. Honest conclusions that admit unexpected results — and try to explain them — score higher than ones that twist the evidence to fit the prediction.

Stage 6 — Evaluating the Enquiry

Evaluation has three main targets: methods, data and conclusions. For each, judge what was strong, what was weak, and how it could be improved.

Ask whether your sampling method gave a representative picture. Was random sampling really random, or did you skip awkward sites? Was systematic sampling spaced widely enough to catch local variation? Was your sample size large enough? On a beach pebble study, 30 pebbles per site is a common minimum — fewer than that and a single oddly shaped pebble can swing the mean.

Equipment also matters. A clinometer reading is only as accurate as the person using it. Tape measures stretch in heat. Questionnaires are biased if you only ask people on a sunny weekend. Pin down the source of any error rather than just saying ‘readings could have been more accurate’.

Reliability, Bias and Accuracy

Three key terms come up in every Eduqas evaluation question. Accuracy is how close your measurement was to the real value. Reliability is whether the same method would give similar results if repeated. Bias is a systematic distortion — for example, only surveying shoppers on a Saturday morning gives a misleading picture of the high street as a whole.

Key Fact

Accuracy and reliability are not the same thing. A clinometer reading can be accurate but unreliable if only one person can use it correctly. Reliable methods are repeatable; accurate methods are correct. Both are needed for a strong enquiry.

Strengths and Limitations of Data

Evaluation also considers your data sources. Primary data is up-to-date and matched to your specific question, but is limited by the time and weather of the day you collected it. Secondary data covers longer periods and wider areas, but it was collected for someone else’s purpose — so it may not match your sites exactly. Strong evaluations weigh the two, noting that they complement each other.

Stakeholders matter too. The spec reminds us that primary or secondary sources may have vested interests: a tourism board reporting visitor satisfaction has reason to highlight the positive, an environmental group reporting reef damage has reason to highlight the negative. Treat sources critically rather than at face value.

Suggesting Improvements

A good evaluation always ends with realistic improvements. Vague suggestions like ‘take more readings’ gain little credit. Specific ones do: ‘Repeat the survey on a weekday and a weekend so weekly variation is captured.’ ‘Use a metre rule rather than tape measures to reduce stretch error.’ ‘Include both Welsh and English coastal sites to test whether the pattern holds in contrasting environments.’

Applying Ideas to UK Decisions

The final part of the fieldwork paper sets a UK decision-making task. You are given a set of resources — maps, graphs, photographs, news extracts — about a real UK issue such as a coastal management scheme, a wind farm proposal, or a new flood defence. You must read the evidence, weigh the options, and recommend a course of action with reasons.

The skills are the same as for fieldwork: read the data carefully, identify patterns, weigh strengths against limitations, and reach a clear judgement supported by evidence. Strong answers state which option you would choose, give two or three reasons drawn from the resources, then briefly acknowledge the trade-offs of the option you rejected.

Imagine you are given two options for a Norfolk coastline: hold the line with rock armour, or managed retreat. Resources include cost estimates, photographs of cliff retreat, and population data for the village behind the cliffs. A strong answer might recommend managed retreat because the long-term cost is lower, the cliffs are eroding too fast for hard defences to work indefinitely, and a salt marsh would form behind the new shoreline. It would acknowledge that residents lose homes and need fair compensation — an honest trade-off rather than a one-sided recommendation.
before.exam_tip_html: In evaluation questions, examiners look for the words ‘reliability’, ‘accuracy’, ‘bias’, ‘representative’ and ‘sample size’. Drop two or three of these into your answer with a specific example each — not generic statements. For UK decision-making questions, mark a clear recommendation in the first line, give two or three evidence-based reasons, and finish with a one-sentence acknowledgement of the rejected option’s trade-off. SPaG marks reward correct geographical vocabulary throughout.
